'Like a sucker punch': Author's despair as novel appears on pirated database three months before publication
News
Jun 12, 2025
by Matilda Battersby
Harriet Evans
Today (Thursday, 12th June) is publication day for
Harriet Evans’ novel
The Treasures
(Viking). Except, before it even hits bookshelves and nightstands, the novel might well have already been scraped by Meta to train its artificial intelligence.
When US magazine
The Atlantic
published a searchable catalogue of the
pirated database LibGen
used by the Facebook owner in the development of its generative AI chatbot Llama 3, Evans discovered that a novel of hers that wouldn’t be published for another three months had already been pirated.
“When I saw
The Treasures
along with all my other books [on Library Genesis in March] it felt like I’d been punched in the stomach,” she told
The Bookseller
.
The Treasures
is the first in a trilogy acquired by Viking last year. Evans is a bestselling author previously published by Headline and HarperCollins as well as Viking under her own name, and as Harriet F Townson by
Hodder & Stoughton
.
She said discovering a book that was not yet on bookshelves had been pirated on
Library Genesis
– a huge database of stolen books that has been the subject of repeated legal action for copyright infringement – alongside all her other titles was “like a sucker punch”.
“You know that feeling when you’re little and someone pushes you over, and the shock of losing your balance is really destabilising. That’s the only thing I can compare it to,” she said.
“I’ve been a publisher. I have had many books published. I’m on the
Society of Authors
committee, where you see different sides of the industry. I know what AI can do... Still, seeing my unpublished book there, it was honestly like a sucker punch.”
Evans told
The Bookseller
she has no idea how her novel might have been leaked.
“I don’t have a hunch about how it happened, because there are so many possible stages,” she said. “It was sent out on worldwide submission for translation and US rights.”
The version of
The Treasures
that appears on LibGen has the final cover art and appears to have been professionally edited and laid out to high production standards. As a result, Evans thinks the other option is that “at some point in the printing process, someone got hold of the files” – although she “thinks this is unlikely”.
The author doesn’t believe that digital e-reader providers such as Amazon, Apple or Kobo would have had access to the finished book file at the time it was leaked. Evans said she believes another possibility is that the final proofs on LibGen, which are sent to reviewers in advance of publication via NetGalley, may have come from there.
“NetGalley is a major marketing tool for all publishers and I am really, really grateful for it, especially because the books I write don’t tend to be widely reviewed in the press,” she said.
NetGalley disputed a claim that the book could have been leaked from there, as Kristina Radke, senior vice-president of NetGalley, told
The Bookseller
: “NetGalley takes the security of our clients’ files very seriously and we are proud to offer industry-standard protection. We have no evidence to suggest there is a connection between files originating from NetGalley and those that end up on the LibGen database."
Continues...

Screenshot of Harriet Evans' book The Treasures on LibGen
The Bookseller
understands that there are at least two confirmed examples of other books that were leaked to LibGen months prior to publication and the concern is that this is simply the tip of the iceberg.
One editor who declined to be named described the process of emailing final proofs of unpublished books for review as “sending the files out willy-nilly in the hope of review coverage, quotes and word of mouth. Other industries are far more security-conscious.”
She added: “Everything sent me to as a freelancer comes on trust. I rarely, if ever, sign confidentiality agreements. Same for reviewers. And big authors get sent everything in the hope of quotes. When the LibGen story broke, friends in the gaming industry were bemused, as they couldn’t believe we didn’t protect our files as they do.”
Industry insiders told
The Bookseller
they believe there is a knowledge gap when it comes to protecting intellectual property, with a lack of training about how to encrypt files and an assumption that others will abide by the laws of copyright “so they didn’t need to spend money protecting book files”.
The question of how to protect authors’ work comes at a time when the definition of UK copyright is under threat. Earlier this year, the government launched a consultation on a proposed copyright exception to help the training of chatbots – the results of which are yet to be published.
Evans has been working with her editor at Viking/Penguin Random House (PRH) to look into the leak. A spokesperson for PRH told
The Bookseller
: “We firmly believe that the unauthorised ingestion of copyrighted content to train generative AI models is a copyright infringement and we share the deep frustration and concern of our authors.⁠
⁠“We will continue to work closely with the
Publishers Association
and the wider creative industries to call on the government to ensure that the UK’s gold standard copyright regime continues to be protected and respected, so rights holders are fairly rewarded for their work.⁠”
Anna Ganley, CEO of the Society of Authors, told
The Bookseller
: “It is devastating that authors’ copyright-protected works can be so easily pirated online, particularly before they have even been published… When the value of intellectual property is so easily stolen and copyright eroded, why should authors bother investing their time and creative labour into creating it?”
Evans said: “This is everyone’s problem. It is a publisher problem. It is a trade problem. It’s an author problem. This one book feels like the canary in the coal mine, because I suspect it reflects a much, much bigger problem. There needs to be an industry-wide investigation into it.”

We spoke with Washington State Attorney General Nick Brown, one of the few top state officials calling out Trump’s actions for what they are: fascist. In his position, Brown, who recently threatened to sue over the administration’s latest travel ban targeting majority-Black and Brown nations, may soon be one of the only legal guardrails standing between this city and a federal agency unleashed with impunity. He talked with The Stranger about the country’s descent into fascism, his ability to fight against it.
          
            by Marcus Harrison Green
In the last week, while the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement descends on workplaces, thousands across the country have taken to the streets in anti-ICE protests, pushing back against the ideology that
children with brain cancer,
breast cancer survivors
,
parents with newborns
,
third graders
, and
farmers
keeping the economy are more terrorizing than masked federal agents who vanish people off the streets without warning, warrants, or due process.
National headlines fixate on California—where Trump has deployed
4,000 National Guard troops and 700 Marines
in a dystopian show of force even the
LAPD finds alarming
—but Seattle isn’t standing still. There have been protests outside immigration courts throughout the week, and on Saturday, June 14, the same day Trump plans a self-fellating birthday parade to celebrate both his 79th year and ostensibly the 250th anniversary of our imperial war machine, more than 1,800 protests are planned nationwide, including two taking place simultaneously in Seattle: a march from Cal Anderson to Seattle Center and a rally at UW’s Red Square.
Seattleites have every reason to stay alert.
Recent reports
say that the administration has directed ICE to deploy special tactical units in blue cities,
including here,
and it’s been barely a month since
SPD cracked down
on counter-protesters at an anti-LGBTQ rally, while far-right agitators were given a pass. Even as protests erupt nationwide, officer conduct is scrutinized far less than the people they claim to serve and protect.
Against this backdrop, we spoke with Washington State Attorney General Nick Brown, one of the few top state officials calling out Trump’s actions for what they are: fascist. In his position, Brown, who recently threatened to sue over the administration’s latest travel ban targeting majority-Black and Brown nations, may soon be one of the only legal guardrails standing between this city and a federal agency unleashed with impunity. He talked with
The Stranger
about the country’s descent into fascism, his ability to fight against it.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
Washington has historically declared itself a sanctuary state. What does that really mean when federal military units are being used to support ICE? How would you uphold our sanctuary commitments in that context?
Well, I generally avoid using the term “sanctuary” because it means different things to different people, and it’s not defined in any of our laws. That vagueness can be risky in terms of what people think it entails.
What I will say is this: for generations, Washington has been a state that supports immigrant and refugee communities—whether someone has legal status, temporary status, or no status. We’ve reaffirmed, through state policy, that our law enforcement agencies are here to enforce
criminal
law, not civil immigration law. Many local jurisdictions have taken that same approach.
We’ve seen the president try to challenge those kinds of policies elsewhere. His administration even issued a so-called list of "sanctuary jurisdictions" last week—which they quickly retracted because it was riddled with errors.
But I think two things can be true: we can keep our communities safe and enforce our laws without becoming an arm of ICE or the federal government. And honestly, most of the law enforcement officers I’ve spoken to don’t want to be immigration agents. A lot of federal law enforcement officials feel the same way—they’re being pulled into immigration work because the president is fixated on it, instead of focusing on more pressing public safety challenges.
Our laws are under scrutiny, yes, and we’re facing threats. That’s part of why I brought a lawsuit against a county sheriff in Adams County who violated the Keep Washington Working Act. We were in court on that case just today in Spokane, and I feel confident about our path forward. We are committed to defending state sovereignty and making sure our resources are used where they belong—not on attempts to erase immigrants or undocumented people from our communities.
If the federal government were to deploy the National Guard or US Marines to suppress anti-ICE protests in Washington, as has happened in California, what legal recourse would your office pursue to protect the rights of Washingtonians?
As a legal matter, at least from my observation, the president is abusing his authority once again. You can only mobilize the National Guard under very specific conditions—you need both a substantive and procedural basis to do so. From what I can tell, none of the three substantive criteria for doing so are present in this case.
And procedurally, the president is required to work through the Governor’s office. According to all the reporting and the lawsuit California filed, none of that process was followed. So, to me, it appears clearly illegal.
If the same fact pattern were to happen here in Washington, we’d likely be in a very similar legal position to California—and I expect we’d challenge it too. If there were a truly substantive situation that required federal assistance, and if the president followed the law and worked with the Governor here to coordinate deployment, that
might
be legal. But if he acted here as he did in California, we would absolutely challenge it.
Can the Attorney General’s Office intervene if federal authorities begin detaining activists or organizers under the guise of “national security” or “immigration enforcement”? What limits (if any) exist on that power?
Yes and yes.
First, I think it's essential that people continue to protest and have their voices heard. Communities are rightly energized and scared right now—and they should not cower in the face of that fear. We need to preserve the spirit of protest, but we also have to be smart about how we do it. We don’t want to hand the president an excuse to escalate things, as he has in California.
We’re monitoring what’s happening in other states and doing everything we can to support our partners, including the Governor’s office. We're trying to assess what might unfold this weekend. Now, we don’t represent individuals, but we
do
have a duty to defend state law and state authority. If federal officials violate our laws or people's rights, we have a role to play. What that looks like will depend on the specifics.
Look, immigration enforcement has existed for over a century. Previous administrations, including Biden’s and those before him, have deported people. But what we’re seeing now is something different. It’s authoritarian. We're talking about people being kidnapped off the street, visas revoked for speaking out, workplace raids that disregard human dignity. That demands a much more urgent and active response from state officials.
Are you in communication with city attorneys or local mayors about a united legal response should ICE, CBP, or the military begin coordinating actions in their jurisdictions?
Not specifically in response to what might happen this week, but yes—we’re in regular communication, especially with larger jurisdictions where more of this activity tends to occur. I spoke with the Mayor this morning about the situation in California and what that might signal for us.
Sometimes we join legal challenges together. More often, we coordinate with other states on lawsuits, since each AG has different responsibilities. Information-sharing and collaboration are important, even if we’re not always signing on to the same litigation.
This county has a long and painful history of federal force being used to suppress Black, Indigenous, immigrant, and working-class communities—from the civil rights movement to Standing Rock. Have you taken any lessons from that history in shaping your approach today?
Absolutely. I was really struck this morning watching the president say that protesters will be met with “huge force.” We’ve gotten numb to his rhetoric, but we shouldn't be.
The idea of a president so reflexively opposed to protest and First Amendment rights—especially in light of our history—is terrifying. The communities most targeted by authoritarianism are always the most vulnerable. Trump has built his political career on attacking communities of color, dehumanizing marginalized people, and fostering a culture that legitimizes hate.
One of the reasons I value being a lawyer is because, during the civil rights era, the courts were a bedrock of progress. The Supreme Court was—at times—an institution the Black community could turn to for protection of our rights. We’re not in that moment now. The Court is moving in the wrong direction. But the legacy of
Brown v. Board of Education
, of district judges ruling in favor of the least powerful—that matters. It shows what’s possible.
That’s why I believe attorneys general have a vital role right now. We have tools to fight back. I said this recently, and I don’t say it lightly, but I don’t know how anyone can look at the last five months and not start to see fascism. The suppression of dissent, the rewriting of history, the targeting of opponents—these are textbook signs. We have to oppose this with every legal and moral tool we have.
I recently spoke with a woman—she's been a US citizen for over 40 years. English isn’t her first language, and she told me she’s scared to leave her home. She’s brown-skinned, and for the first time, she said she’s afraid to attend a protest because she might be profiled, abducted, or disappeared. So this is less a question for the attorney general and more for you as a citizen: What would you say to someone like her—someone who feels like the government no longer protects them, and maybe never did?
First, I’d say: this moment is
not
her responsibility.
People like her shouldn’t have to carry the burden of fixing this. I don’t want to minimize her fear—it’s absolutely real. When the president, the Secretary of Defense, and the US Attorney General are all leaning into authoritarianism, the last thing we should do is expect those most at risk to stand on the front lines.
We
will
get past Trump. This country will survive. But our moral fabric—that can unravel quickly. And it’s going to take more than lawyers to repair it.
Those of us in safer positions must step up. We have to be the voices for those who are afraid. We have to tell the truth about what’s happening—loudly and often—because we’re already losing our grip on it.

Democrat-Leaning Firms Reveal Just How Bad Dems Are Polling On Immigration
GUILLERMO ARIAS/AFP via Getty Images
Jason Hopkins
Immigration Reporter
June 12, 2025
4:55 PM ET
June 12, 2025 4:55 PM ET
Jason Hopkins
Immigration Reporter
Font Size:
A newly-released survey illustrates just how poorly Americans view the Democratic Party’s job performance on immigration.
Only 19% of likely voters in swing districts across the U.S. approve of Democrats’ handling on immigration,
according to
a poll released Thursday by Way to Win and Impact Research. Seventy-seven percent of these likely voters disapprove of the party’s handing on immigration, giving Democrats a 58-point net negative rating on the issue.
(RELATED: Trump Admin’s War Against Sanctuary States Escalates With New Lawsuit)
Way to Win and Impact Research, both of which are Democratic-leaning firms, conducted the survey in order to help the party find the right messaging strategy to chip away at the GOP’s advantage on immigration, according to POLITICO, which
first obtained
the poll.
Republicans are also underwater on immigration, but to a significantly smaller degree, according to the survey. The GOP has an 11-point negative job rating on the issue, with 43% approving and 54% disapproving of their handling on immigration.
OLMITO, TEXAS – FEBRUARY 29: President Joe Biden speaks with a U.S. Customs and Border Protection officer during a presentation about immigration and border security at the Brownsville Station on February 29, 2024 in Olmito, Texas. (Photo by Cheney Orr/Getty Images)
“Democrat support is at rock bottom, and they need to rebuild their trust on this issue,” the authors of the poll concluded. [President Donald Trump’s] overall job rating is negative by a 5-point margin in districts he collectively won by two points, but voters are slightly more favorable on how he’s handled immigration and the policies he and Republicans have enacted.”
“And while Republicans in Congress are underwater by double digits on immigration, they are still in significantly better shape here than Democrats in Congress, whose popularity and trust on immigration are worse by wide margins,” the authors continued.
The poll was conducted from May 6 to 11, and includes a margin-of-error of plus or minus 3.1%.
The survey comes in the wake of President Joe Biden’s tenure over the worst immigration crisis in U.S. history — and Trump’s subsequent efforts to close the border and enforce large-scale deportations.
Illegal immigration into the U.S. exploded under the Biden administration, with fiscal years 2023 and 2024 being the two worst years for total migrant encounters,
according to
Customs and Border Protection data. The average number of monthly border encounters during the Biden-era nearly reached 160,000 and the daily average peaked at 15,000,
according to
Department of Homeland Security data.
Over the course of the 46th president’s four years in office, Customs and Border Protection recorded roughly 11 million border encounters — a wave of immigration that
severely strained
federal and local resources at the time and moved Americans
to the right
on immigration. Trump won re-election in November while pledging to close the southern border and deport criminal illegal migrants.

Democratic Senators Elizabeth Warren and Richard Blumenthal issued a letter to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, raising concerns over reports that the tech giant is once again exploring the launch of its own stablecoin.
In the letter, the senators warn that Meta’s renewed interest in digital currency, reminiscent of its failed Libra and Diem initiatives, could pose serious risks to financial privacy, economic competition, and national monetary sovereignty.
Zuckerberg Pressed on Stablecoin Strategy
Citing recent reports that Meta has been in discussions with crypto firms and hired a fintech executive to lead its stablecoin push, the lawmakers
argued
that any such move, whether through direct issuance or strategic partnership, would allow the company to tighten its grip over payments across its massive 3.5-billion-user ecosystem.
The senators express concern that a Meta-backed stablecoin could allow deeper surveillance of user transactions, threaten competition, and expose consumers to systemic financial instability. Drawing parallels with the 2023 depegging of USDC and the subsequent federal backstop, they warn that taxpayers may again be forced to shoulder the consequences of a run on a Meta-linked stablecoin.
Beyond financial risk, the letter also outlined the company’s history of privacy violations, antitrust investigations, and failure to safeguard users, especially children, from harm, and argued that such a record makes the company uniquely unfit to manage a private currency system.
The timing of the company’s revived stablecoin ambition is also significant, coming as Congress debates the GENIUS Act, which could pave the way for Big Tech to issue digital dollars through lightly regulated affiliates. Warren and Blumenthal question whether Meta is lobbying lawmakers to influence the bill’s language and seek clarification on whether the company is trying to exploit regulatory loopholes to gain a controlling stake in a stablecoin issuer.
Meta Faces June 17 Deadline
The letter also demands detailed disclosures by June 17, including a list of consulted crypto firms, intended platforms for deployment, and lobbying activity related to the
GENIUS
and STABLE Acts. The senators have called on the tech company to explain how its current stablecoin plans differ from the
Libra and Diem
projects and what steps have been taken to address past concerns.
In a clear pushback against what they see as a dangerous overreach, the lawmakers ask whether it would support amendments to block Big Tech firms from issuing or controlling stablecoins explicitly.
The post
Senators Slam Meta’s Stablecoin Push, Cite Privacy Risks and Regulatory Loopholes
appeared first on
CryptoPotato
.

Hodderscape and Lucy’s Book Club launch fantasy event series
News
Jun 12, 2025
by Isabel Dempsey
Lucy Ellis
Hodderscape
, the science fiction and fantasy imprint of
Hodder & Stoughton
, has announced a new collaboration with Lucy’s Book Club to launch a series of intimate, community-led events celebrating the best in
fantasy fiction
.
Designed as a cosy, connected space for readers to meet new friends, swap books and get lost in their favourite magical worlds, the events will be held in collaboration with
independent bookshops
.
Each event will centre around a different fantasy title, promising signature cocktails inspired by the books, games designed to help readers meet their next bookish best friend, and an unfiltered, joyful discussion about their favourite fantasy reads.
The first event will take place on Wednesday 2nd July at Bourne & Hollingsworth Buildings, and will spotlight the romantasy book of the moment:
Quicksilver
by
Callie Hart
. Tickets for the first event will go on sale on Tuesday 17th June.
Founder of Lucy’s Book Club, Lucy Ellis, said: “I started the book club to create a safe space for people with a shared love of reading to connect. When I first launched it, I never imagined I’d end up working with the very people who bring these books to life, let alone with a publisher like Hodder. One of the most frequent requests I get is to choose a fantasy book for the club. Until now, I’ve never had the opportunity to explore fantasy novels with my community, so I am excited to create a space where fantasy lovers feel truly welcome.”
Marketing manager at Hodder, Laura Bartholomew, said: “I’ve followed Lucy’s Book Club for a while now, and I love seeing how she brings readers together with warmth, humour and impeccable taste – creating a beautiful community of readers. It’s a dream to establish the partnership between Hodderscape and Lucy’s Book Club to help bring a little extra magic to the Book Club experience and introduce readers to exciting, new worlds.”
Senior publicity manager, Kate Keehan, said :“Hodderscape began as a digital space for readers to connect through their love of fantastical fiction. Partnering with Lucy’s Book Club feels like an extension of that connection and community that’s always powered our imprint. We’re so excited to introduce new readers to the worlds within our favourite stories.”

E Lockhart promises 'expanded' storylines and characters in We Were Liars adaptation
News
Jun 12, 2025
by Caroline Carpenter
We Were Liars: (l-r) Emily Alyn Lind, Esther McGregor, Joseph Zada and Shubham Maheshwari as the four titular Liars
Amazon Prime’s upcoming adaptation of
We Were Liars
(Hot Key Books) will “flesh out” the characters and storylines in E Lockhart’s bestselling YA novel, the author has told
The Bookseller
.
Psychological thriller
We Were Liars
centres on Cadence, a member of the seemingly perfect Sinclair family. It sees her return to the private island her family spends every summer on two years after suffering a serious head injury. There, she tries to remember what happened to her and the rest of the gang the family refers to as “The Liars” – her cousins Johnny and Mirren and her first love, Gat. The author hopes that the show will “bring people to my books, and I hope the books bring people to the show”. She added: “I think that they’re two different expressions of the same story… Watching the show is going to give you an expanded idea of what’s in the book. I think they’re going to complement each other really well.”
The book was published in 2014 to critical acclaim and commercial success, and this adaptation has been a long time coming. “
We Were Liars
has been in development for film or television since it was published, so there has been a very long process of setting it up, first at one studio, then at another, and so forth,” explained Lockhart. “When Julie Plec and Carina Adly MacKenzie signed on to do it, I was really thrilled, because this was the first situation where I knew who was going to be writing and showrunning the project from the very first conversation about Universal and Prime Video acquiring it. They make this incredible, bingeable television, and they love the book. Their expertise and enthusiasm was unlike any of the development experiences I’d had before.”
As an executive producer on the show, Lockhart was “super involved” with the early part of the location scouting and the casting. Emily Alyn Lind stars as Cadence, with Shubham Maheshwari, Joseph Zada (recently announced as the lead of next year’s
Hunger Games film
) and Esther McGregor playing her fellow Liars. Lockhart joked that the cast is “so much better looking than I ever imagined”.
Reflecting on other differences between the book and show, she said: “The novel is in first person, so nothing is going on in
We Were Liars
that the heroine doesn’t see and know about. But on television, everything is expanded and opened up, so people are going to get to see stories for characters that are really fleshed out.” Four writers of Indian descent joined the writers’ room to bring their lived experience to “deeper storylines” for the characters of Gat and his Uncle Ed. Johnny, Mirren and the mother characters – played by Mamie Gummer, Caitlin FitzGerald and Candice King – all have expanded storylines too, which Lockhart predicts her readers will be “really psyched to see”.
Continues...

We Were Liars tells the story of Cadence, who is trying to remember what happened to her before a serious head injury
The series’ pilot was shot by cinematographer Simon Duggan, who has previously worked on films including Baz Lurhmann’s The Great Gatsby and Furiosa, and “designed the look of the whole show”.
Lockhart promises that viewers will feel an “incredible sense of coming to Beechwood Island... We have the most gorgeous scenery, so I think the feeling of immersion in this beautiful world is going to be very thrilling.” She added: “We have a really exceptional cast... I think we absolutely deliver a big story about first love with a lot of humour and nuance.”
Lockhart spent 10 weeks on set, which she found “a very intense experience – it was like the heroes and the villains of my imagination were walking all around me”. She added: “That was a huge learning curve for me, the long hours and the intense collaboration that’s happening not just with the show runners, but also with the costumers and the production assistants and the actors and the cinematographers. It was very meaningful to be part of a big team all pulling for the same result.”
She also penned the show’s final episode. “I had written for TV and movies a bit, but this was the first thing I’ve written that has been filmed… I worked with the team of writers on the show to outline the episode and all the things that would happen. It’s the same story as the book, but for a TV show you really need an outline, and everything needs to come to a satisfying conclusion.” Comparing screenwriting to authoring a book, she said: “When you write a novel, the novel is all yours. When you write an episode of television, you are collaborating on the structure with a whole room full of people, and you are also handing it over to your show runners for final touches, any revisions that they need to make to make the whole season cohere. So you have to be flexible, you have to be cheerful and just be there for the adventure.”
Continues...
We Were Liars: the Sinclair family spend every summer on their private island
Despite being published more than a decade ago,
We Were Liars
has experienced a second wave of popularity in recent years thanks to TikTok, where the hashtag #wewereliars has been used nearly 21,000 times.
“I had no idea that any of this was happening online. My publisher didn’t either,” admitted Lockhart. “During the pandemic, so many creators were making videos on TikTok, some of which were incredibly carefully edited and produced. This just started happening organically, and by the time I knew about it, I was on the bestseller list again.
“I feel incredibly grateful that other people chose to exercise their creativity on my book, and that that led other people to read it. That doesn’t mean all those people liked the book. Sometimes they wanted to throw it across the room. They always had some kind of visceral emotional reaction to the book, though, and that was very satisfying.”
Lockhart believes that the novel provokes such reactions due to its combination of the aspirational nature of its setting and characters, and the familiarity of the issues they face. She explained: “I’ve set these people up as some kind of American royalty, playing out real everyday problems – competition among children, falling in love for the first time, disagreements between parents and children, intense friendships, huge emotions, family strife. These are things that happen to teenagers in all kinds of families and social situations all across the globe all the time… So, I think it’s simultaneously a fantasy of this beautiful private island and a lot of wealth, and also very relatable.”
Lockhart recently announced a third book set in the world of
We Were Liars
, following the publication of prequel
Family of Liars
in 2022. Standalone novel
We Fell Apart
will be published by Hot Key Books in November 2025. Its timeline overlaps with that of
We Were Liars
. Lockhart is “super psyched” about the book, which she describes as a “Gothic” story with “a mysterious beach house and an intense love story, if I’ve done it right”. It focuses on Matilda, who discovers a father she’s never met – a reclusive artist who asks her to spend the summer at his seaside home. But when she arrives, he is not there and instead she finds her long-lost brother Meer, former child star Brock and brooding Tatum, who just wants her to leave their crumbling sanctuary. Matilda must delve into the twisted heart of the estate to uncover the answers she’s desperately craving, but “everybody there is hiding secrets and lying to her”.
When asked if she will return to the world of
We Were Liars
again, Lockhart teased: “I might. I’m not making any promises, though.”

ILOILO CITY, Philippines – Civil society groups in Antique have called on newly-appointed Environment Secretary Raphael Lotilla to reject a proposed 3,715-hectare mineral reservation in Antique, warning of the environmental consequences of opening upland towns to large-scale mining.
The Amlig Alliance Antique, a coalition of local organizations, has appealed to Lotilla to block the proposal of the Mines and Geosciences Bureau (MGB), which seeks to classify parts of the towns of Patnongon, San Remigio, Valderrama, and Sibalom as mineral reserves due to deposits of copper, gold, and chromite.
In May, Lotilla, a former Energy secretary, was
tapped to replace Maria Antonia Yulo-Loyzaga
as head of the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR),
In a letter dated June 2, the alliance framed its appeal around the Antique-born Lotilla’s personal connection to the province, invoking his roots and identity.
“We write to you not just as the DENR Secretary, but as a son of Sibalom – one who knows the sacredness of our land and the fragility of our mountains,” wrote lawyer Rolly Pedrina, chairperson of the alliance.
Lotilla, born in Sibalom on June 16, 1958, took over the DENR amid renewed debates over mining’s role in the economy versus its long-term social and ecological impacts.
The MGB’s proposal is grounded in national policy to secure strategic raw materials and promote mineral development, which includes the possibility of exploration and extraction under state oversight. A mineral reservation may only be established through a presidential proclamation, following a recommendation from the DENR secretary and the MGB.
But locals feared the designation would pave the way for extractive operations in fragile upland ecosystems.
“This is the moment your (Lotilla) covenant with Antique must be proven,” Pedrina added.
As of February 2022, at least 12 exploration permit applications remain pending within the proposed reserve area.
Environmental advocates said permits are typically the first step toward larger agreements, including Mineral Production Sharing Agreements (MPSA) and Financial or Technical Assistance Agreements (FTAA), which enable large-scale and often foreign-financed mining.
The alliance has also
called for a 50-year moratorium
on all mining activities in Antique, and urged Lotilla to suspend all pending applications by issuing a department order.
In February, the provincial board passed a resolution formally opposing the MGB’s move, citing environmental and cultural concerns. Local lawmakers pointed to the ecological importance of the Sibalom Watershed, which supports several downstream municipalities including Belison, Hamtic, and the capital town of San Jose de Buenavista.
“The disruption of the area will further put the lives and properties of the Antiqueños at risk, the same communities that suffered devastating losses brought about by Typhoon Frank [and] Severe Tropical Storm Paeng,” the resolution read. Typhoon Frank (Fengshen) in 2008 and Severe Tropical Storm Paeng (Nalgae) in 2022 caused substantial damage in the province.
Municipal councils in the affected areas have passed similar resolutions rejecting the mining proposal.
The Chamber of Mines of the Philippines (COMP), meanwhile, welcomed Lotilla’s appointment, expressing confidence that he would support the mining sector’s expansion while maintaining environmental safeguards.
COMP chairman Michael Toledo said they expected Lotilla to “[maximize] the full potential of the Philippine minerals development industry in improving the lives of present and future generations of Filipinos without compromising the integrity of the environment.” –

On June 12, 1899, a powerful tornado tore through New Richmond, Wisconsin, killing 117 people and devastating the town in what remains one of America’s deadliest tornadoes.
More information:
Rating Tornadoes: The Enhanced Fujita Scale Explained
The June 12, 1899 tornado destroyed over 300 buildings in New Richmond, Wisconsin, killing 117 people in minutes.
Circuses were once among the biggest attractions for small-town America. On a warm summer afternoon in 1899, crowds gathered in
New Richmond, Wisconsin
, for the Gollmar Brothers Circus. What followed would turn the festive day into one of tragedy, leaving a permanent mark on U.S. weather history.
A Twister Strikes at the Worst Time
The day began with
above-average temperatures
and high humidity, typical of early summer in the Upper Midwest. With the arrival of the Gollmar Brothers Circus, New Richmond’s population temporarily surged, drawing large crowds into the town center.
As the big top emptied and visitors strolled the streets, a funnel cloud approached the town. Originating as a
waterspout over Lake St. Croix,
the tornado roared into Wisconsin, flattening farms near Burkhardt and Boardman before taking direct aim at New Richmond. Around 4:30 PM, the tornado ripped through the heart of the town,
leveling over 300 buildings
in its path.
June 12th, 1899 = One of the most tragic weather events in Wisconsin's history.
New Richmond Tornado
The 9th deadliest tornado in US history
https://t.co/S9q9hpenzm
pic.twitter.com/guuqPpa6Sk
— Don Penim (@Don_Penim)
June 12, 2025
The storm carved a path estimated to be
1,000 feet wide
and nearly three-quarters of a mile long. A 3,000-pound safe was hurled a full city block, while entire families
were killed as buildings crumbled around them. In total,
117 people lost their lives and over 150 others were injured
—many by flying debris.
Survivors Recall the Storm’s Fury
New Richmond resident Anna Epley described
two cloud masses merging into a funnel
that “boiled within itself” as it hugged the ground and raced toward town. Its visibility may have given some time to flee—though many had no chance to react.
“The day had been
unseasonably warm, clear and sunny until about 3 p.m., when the sky clouded darkly,” Epley later recounted in the
Milwaukee Journal
. “At 4:30 it began to rain, stopping after about 20 minutes. The sky became still darker. Then the murderous cone of wind swirled in, tearing homes and business blocks from their foundations, hurling timber and uprooted trees like javelins in every direction, sweeping men and women from their feet and crushing them against walls or the ground.”
Other first-hand accounts described bark-stripped trees, tin roofing twisted around trunks, and debris scattered across the city.
The New Richmond tornado of 1899 was the deadliest in state history and the 9th deadliest in the country. 117 people died, 150 were hurt, and much of the city had to be rebuilt.
#wiwx
pic.twitter.com/hUNF21qttn
— Wisconsin State Climatology Office (@WI_ClimateSCO)
April 10, 2025
Survivors searched through rubble as fires broke out, adding to the destruction left in the tornado’s wake.
A Broader Path of Destruction
Though New Richmond was hit hardest, the storm’s reach stretched beyond. Reports from
Hastings, Minnesota
, suggest the tornado's roots may have extended farther southwest. Meanwhile, severe storms drenched areas like
La Crosse and Winona
, where
flash floods
washed away bridges and forced families to evacuate by boat.
Related article
A Tornado Makes the Perfect Backdrop for a Couple's Wedding Photos
This combination of tornadic and flood damage made
June 1899
one of the most destructive periods in Wisconsin’s recorded weather history. To this day, the New Richmond tornado remains
the ninth deadliest tornado on record in the United States
, a somber reminder of how quickly weather can turn catastrophic.

CHICAGO - Dozens of Chicago teens recently crossed the graduation stage with more than a diploma in their hands.
Every year, dozens of young fathers between the ages of 17 and 24 go through a special graduation. While it looks similar to any other graduation, this ceremony is as significant to the child in the audience as the father walking across the stage.
In a classroom along South Cottage Grove, the curriculum has been life-changing.
Pit bull sisters inspire tolerance, kindness at CPS schools
"To have this program was a godsend," Ahmad Shipp of the Dovetail Project said. "This program gave me a lot of reasons to keep going when a lot of times I didn't want to, when I didn't see a way out."
Shipp sat in the second row of the classroom made up of young fathers.
"I grew up with two teen parents," Dovetail Project Founder Sheldon Smith said. "And seeing many of my friends across the City of Chicago with that same struggle, it led me to really think just about something that could make our community better."
The program teaches the young fathers three important things. In the words of Smith, those are "parenting skills, life skills and felony street law."
Norte Dame student’s legacy lives on in graduation journey of Chicago’s youth
The Dovetail Project started in 2009 with just nine students. It has now impacted over 730 fathers.
"[It helps] dads get the tools and resources needed to be present in their children's lives, which is extremely important," Smith said.
This year's graduating class donned caps and gowns for the Dovetail Project's 29th graduation ceremony.
"I never got to walk except for eighth grade grad or kindergarten. So now that I get this chance and my son and my family get to see it," Shipp said.
Read more: Latest Chicago news and headlines
Through the Dovetail Project, the young dads found their way.
Last month, the Dovetail Project learned they are the recipient of a grant from the NBA Foundation with support from the Chicago Bulls. The hope is that they will have even more dad grads walking the stage next year.

Humpback whales have long been blowing bubbles, but new research shows that some particular bubbles might only be associated with communicating with us, humans.
Humpback whales are approaching boats and humans then blowing bubble rings to communicate.
It’s not a hello or a wave–it’s a
bubble ring
! And those rings might be a way that humpback whales are trying to
communicate with the humans around them
. Researchers from the SETI Institute in California have documented whales blowing bubble rings during friendly encounters with humans and published their findings in a new paper in
Marine Mammal Science
.
A Fun Communication Tactic
Humans have long been
fascinated by whales
, watching them from the shore and boats, often snapping pictures and shouting. Whales have been known to
approach people and boats
.
This new research shows that the whales are likely
playfully communicating
with the humans they interact with by
blowing bubble rings
in their direction.
“Humpback whales often exhibit inquisitive, friendly behavior towards boats and human swimmers,” said Jodi Frediani, co-lead author and marine wildlife photographer. “We’ve now located a dozen whales from populations around the world, the majority of which have voluntarily approached boats and swimmers blowing bubble rings during these episodes of curious behavior.”
Analyzing Bubbles in the Ocean
The researchers analyzed
12 different bubble ring episodes
that resulted in 39 rings from 11 humpback whales for their report. These events were gathered from various types of vessels and came from researchers, citizen scientists and naturalists.
Bubbles have often been associated with
humpback whale behavio
r. For instance, males use bubbles on breeding grounds and mothers and calves have been observed exhaling blowhole bubbles. Then there are the
bubble nets
where an individual whale or multiple whales create an air curtain of bubbles as they spiral in on their prey.
Picture of at least one bubble ring from each episode used in the study. Image Credit: Sharpe et al. Mar. Mam. Sci. 2025.
“Humpback whales live in complex societies, are acoustically diverse, use bubble tools and assist other species being harassed by predators,” said co-lead author Dr. Fred Sharpe.
But when it comes to specific bubble rings, these have only been associated with human interactions.
The researchers used observations from drones over multiple years to see if bubble rings like the ones observed by humans were produced when people weren’t around. And they weren’t.
Throughout nearly
5000 drone flights, no bubble rings were detected
. According to the researchers, this means that bubble rings are likely to be selective to when humans were around. However, why they do this is still unknown.
“We show they are blowing bubble rings in our direction in an apparent attempt to playfully interact, observe our response, and/or engage in some form of communication.” Dr Sharpe concluded.
Studying Whales To Find Extraterrestrial Life
The Whale-SETI team is continuing to watch and document bubble ring production to understand the way that whales communicate.
Related article
Giants of the Sea in Action: Whales' Incredible Contribution to Ocean Health
The researchers also noted that studying intelligent, non-terrestrial (aquatic), nonhuman communication systems could also
aid in the search for extraterrestrial life
. They aim to develop a filter that could
parse cosmic signals
to find it.
News Reference
Humpback Whales Blow Poloidal Vortex Bubble Rings
. Marine Mammal Science, Sharpe et al. 2025.

CHICAGO (
WGN
) — The man charged in the death of
Chicago police officer Krystal Rivera
appeared before a Cook County judge on Thursday.
During a brief appearance in Cook County Criminal Court, 25-year-old Adrian Rucker's public defender got permission from the judge to move Thursday’s status hearing for his client to Friday. Post-hearing, the mother and aunt of Rucker told WGN News that they still have questions for investigators concerning the June 5 incident on the city’s South Side.
"We're waiting for bodycam footage," Monique Reed, Rucker's aunt, said.
Authorities said the deadly shooting unfolded shortly before 10 p.m. as CPD officers pursued Rucker, who allegedly fled from a nearby investigatory stop at an apartment near E. 82nd St. and S. Drexel Avenue.
According to CPD, Rivera and another police officer chased an armed Rucker into a unit. Prosecutors say Rucker fled down a hallway and bodycam video captures the suspect pointing an AR pistol, but not firing it.
‘Young, vibrant and a hard worker’: CPD officer dies in South Side shooting
Fallen CPD officer remembered for courage and compassion by loved ones and colleagues
"He never had a rifle," Reed said. "Never had a gun. No gun was found on him."
While 36-year-old Officer Rivera chased the initial suspect, the officer with her accidentally fired his weapon, striking and killing the four-year veteran of Chicago police.
"My condolences to her family, but my nephew is not responsible for her death," Reed said.
Along with serving as part of the Sixth District’s tactical team, those who knew Officer Rivera remembered her as a loving mom who was known for her courage and compassion.
Inside the unit on Drexel, investigators say they found three guns, suspected narcotics, and multiple fake IDs with Rucker’s picture. The 25-year-old of Freeport —a town west of Rockford— faces multiple felonies, including armed violence, illegal possession of a firearm, and illegal drug possession.
Monique Reed says her nephew doesn’t live in the apartment where the shooting occurred.
"I feel like he's being railroaded right now," she said. "We have his side of the story."
Court documents say the armed suspect Officer Rivera and the other officer were chasing last Thursday got away. WGN News reached out to Chicago police to learn if the department is continuing its search, but has not yet heard back.
Read more: Latest Chicago news and headlines
Funeral arrangements for Officer Rivera are pending.

WASHINGTON (NEXSTAR) - California Senator Alex Padilla was forcibly removed from Secretary Kristi Noem’s news conference in Los Angeles, where she was praising law enforcement for cracking down on protests against ICE raids.
"I was forced to the ground, and I was handcuffed,” said Padilla.
Padilla said he wanted to question Noem.
"You can only imagine what they're doing to farmers to cooks to day laborers out in the Los Angeles community and throughout California and throughout the country,” said Padilla.
Noem criticized the interruption during her immigration press conference praising law enforcement.
"I think everybody in America would, would agree that that was inappropriate,” said Noem.
DHS called the move political theater and said Noem and Padilla met after for 15 minutes.
Senate Democrats are up in arms over the removal of their colleague.
"This is something that we should not tolerate,” said Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.).
Democrats demanded an investigation and called out the action taken against the senator.
"If this is how a United States Senator can be treated, then none of us ultimately are immune,” said Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.).
However, Georgia Republican Congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene says what the senator did is against the law.
"It looked very aggressive. Looks like he was attacking the Secretary of Homeland Security. And, he was attacking police officers,” said Greene.
Senate Republican Leader John Thune says they want the facts on what happened before issuing a response.

Media footage advances the investigation into the attack on Colombian Senator Miguel Uribe, pointing to a broader criminal network. Credit: Colombian National Police. (File photo)
Following the attack on Senator and presidential candidate Miguel Uribe in Bogota,
Colombia
, and with no official findings yet released, media investigation suggest the involvement of a criminal network comprising at least six individuals.
According to footage aired yesterday by the local television channel Caracol, five additional people—besides the teenage gunman who carried out the shooting—were present and involved at the scene of the attack.
Using a compilation of videos from security cameras and cell phones of attendees at the political rally, the television channel produced a reconstruction of the moments leading up to the gunshots that left the senator in critical condition at a hospital in the Colombian capital.
Investigation points to criminal network behind attack on Senator Miguel Uribe
While Colombian police and security forces continue to search for those behind the attack, video footage has enabled an alleged reconstruction of the sequence of events. This reconstruction suggests that, in addition to the 14-year-old shooter, at least five other individuals were involved in the attempt on Senator Uribe’s life.
In a series of videos obtained by Colombian television, footage shows the minor arriving on a motorcycle at a location a few blocks from where the senator and presidential candidate was scheduled to appear.
To avoid interfering with the police investigation, Colombian television blurred the faces of those involved while reconstructing—using security and cellphone footage—a timeline spanning over two hours, depicting how the suspects prepared for the attack.
The reconstruction identifies two cars and a total of six individuals directly involved in the operation. Although no official details have been released, President Gustavo Petro formally requested assistance yesterday from
U.S. agencies
to help clarify the case.
The
FBI
confirmed that the pistol used in the attack was legally purchased in Arizona and traveled through Florida before reaching Colombia. How the weapon entered the country, and what connection—if any—the original U.S. purchaser had to its transport, remains unclear.
Video footage reconstructs attack on senator Miguel Uribe
The Colombian television news program presented a possible reconstruction of the hours leading up to the June 7 attack in Bogota, based on a compilation of various video recordings.
The first footage, timestamped at 3:22 p.m.—two hours before the shooting—shows the teenage assailant getting off a motorcycle. He removes his helmet, puts on a cap, briefly speaks with the driver, and makes a phone call.
At 3:41 p.m., a silver vehicle parks near the scene. Five minutes later, the minor is seen approaching the car and speaking with its occupants. After a short exchange, he again uses his cellphone.
Later, at 5:20 p.m., another camera captures a gray car driving along the main avenue near the neighborhood where the attack occurred. The vehicle parks five blocks from the park where Senator Miguel Uribe Turbay was addressing supporters.
At 5:22 p.m., the teenager exits the car, now wearing different clothing than in the earlier footage. He is accompanied by a man wearing a white shirt, black glasses, and a beard, and a woman dressed in a black jacket and carrying a white purse. The three walk together toward the park where the senator is located.
By 5:26 p.m., the youth positions himself behind the presidential candidate, standing in a spot that provided a clear shot. At that moment, only two bodyguards were present, and neither was covering Uribe’s back.
Moments later, the shooting took place. One bullet struck the senator in the head and another in the leg, leaving him in critical condition.
At the end of the reconstruction, another individual is seen fleeing. During the shooting, they run into a nearby restaurant, lock themselves inside with employees, and later leave the scene in a vehicle. Their possible involvement in the attack remains under investigation.
En video quedó registrado el momento en el que las autoridades capturan al sicario que atentó contra la vida de Miguel Uribe (
@MiguelUribeT
), quien además se encontraba con arma de fuego y amenazó con disparar a los policías.
pic.twitter.com/NJSp0mrMj1
— Kienyke (@kienyke)
June 8, 2025
Teenage hitman is the only suspect in custody
Five days after the attack, the teen who carried the assassination attempt is the only person under arrest. He was detained minutes later following a brief police chase through the streets of Bogota.
Despite the video footage from the moments leading up to the attack and the images broadcast by the media that same Saturday, the teenager was not in possession of a cellphone when he was apprehended.
While being restrained on the ground, he spoke to police officers, telling them he “did it for money” and agreed to cooperate. “I can give you the numbers,” he said—allegedly referring to the phone numbers of others involved.
The teenager was shot in the leg during the arrest and is currently recovering at a clinic in Bogota. Because he is under 18, he is being processed under Colombia’s Adolescent Criminal Responsibility System, facing charges of attempted homicide and illegal possession of a firearm.
For now, the country is still in shock. The senator’s
health condition
remains stable and critical, despite slight signs of positive response to yesterday’s surgical interventions.
At the same time,
political tension
remains high, with the government an opposition maintaining confrontational stances that offer little cause for optimism.

ALBANY, N.Y. (NEWS10)---Governor Kathy Hochul was one of three governors before the U.S. House Oversight Committee taking questions from multiple Congressional members on both sides of the aisle about the state’s immigration and sanctuary city policies.
In her opening statement to Congressional members, Governor Kathy Hochul spoke about immigration.
"Our nation needs comprehensive immigration reform from this body, and our state laws dictate we cooperate with ICE in criminal cases," said Hochul." And our values dictate we treat all law-abiding people with dignity and respect."
North Country Congresswoman Elise Stefanik, who is considering a gubernatorial run against Hochul, confronted her with the names of individuals involved in criminal cases.
"Do you know who Sakir Akkahn is? You should, as the Governor of New York State. Do you know?," asked Stefanik.
"Refresh my recollection," said Hochul.
"He was an illegal migrant in New York. Do you know what crime he committed in addition to being here illegally?"
When Hochul said she didn't, Stefanik said he raped a 15-year-old girl in Albany, New York.
In a back and forth with Hochul, Stefanik said, "We deserve a Governor who stands up abiding New Yorkers, doesn’t put illegals first but law-abiding New Yorkers."
Hochul replied, "Rather than going after the viral moment, I suggest you look at the facts."
Western New York Republican Congressman Nick Langworthy also criticized Hochul’s leadership as well as New York’s green light law. According to the DMV, the law allows for people to apply for drivers licenses regardless of their lawful status.
"This is an abomination. This is not keeping New Yorkers safe," said Langworthy.
Hochul responded by saying, "We turn over the information you’re referring to, all the time you’re misstating the laws and its purpose. We cooperate all the time."
"As much as I want to believe you," said Langworthy, "I believe the cops more."
Later in the hearing, Hochul got emotional about the importance of immigrants to communities and the economy.
"They are so critical to our identity and existence. I’m really hurt. It hurts me as a leader of a state that people are living in fear and in the shadows. People can’t go to school, can’t worship, can’t get health care. Can’t go to their senior center. What’s happening has been traumatic and unnecessary. We will help every day of the week to get rid of people who commit crimes that who never should have come her or commit crimes here," said Hochul. "That is my number one job."

) -- Crews were still on scene Thursday after a historic building in Albany was demolished on Tuesday. The Historic Albany Foundation said this building held great history in the city.
Get the latest news, weather, sports and entertainment delivered right to your inbox!
“It's really kind of sad to see all of that go when there was such potential there. The historic character of Albany is really what gives it its flavor," said Cara Macri, director of Preservation Services at The Historic Albany Foundation.
The Historic Albany Foundation makes it their mission to preserve and protect old, historical buildings throughout the city. Macri said Albany is the fourth oldest city in the nation, holding buildings with some of the richest history across the country. This includes Albany's E-Comm buildings on Broadway that were once used as an industrial hot spot. The building that was demolished dates back to the 1800s.
“This building was built in 1849 in this group of buildings that were built just after the Great Fire of 1848 wiped out acres of buildings in downtown Albany," said Macri. “There was a lot happening specifically in that area, it was kind of a shoe, boot, leather, goods district, lots of importing lots of exporting. So that was kind of right in the midst of all of it."
Broadway used to be filled with buildings just like that. However, since then, Macri said many of the buildings have since been demolished after being left vacant for many years.
"It was not unexpected. Two other buildings that were part of that group have come down in the past; one at 50 Hudson Ave came down in 2016, which was much smaller but still a part of that whole group, and another one came down in 2018," said Macri.
Macri believes leaving buildings vacant is a large problem. She said all of the E-Comm buildings have been on the Historic Albany Foundation's endangered building list since 2019.
The Capitalize Albany Corporation currently controls the E-Comm building that was demolished. In part of a statement, President Ashley Mohl cited the weekend's heavy rainfall as part of the reason for the structural damage that led to the demolition.
Colonie PD launches new retail theft unit
"... Following the weekend's heavy rainfall, the Corporation’s property manager visited the eight-acre Liberty Park site and Four E-Comm Square reporting previously unidentified significant structural damage this morning. The property manager had been in this building just two weeks ago, and it was not in this state," said Mohl in part of a statement. "Capitalize Albany contacted the appropriate City of Albany department for an immediate inspection, and city engineers this [Tuesday] afternoon assessed that 4 E-Comm Square is unsafe, irreparable and in danger of collapse."
A spokesperson for the Capitalize Albany Corporation, Michael Bohne said the demolition will cost an estimated $315 million. Bohne also said they are now working to schedule an inspection with the city's codes department for the other buildings they oversee.
A
request for proposals (RFP) process
was recently launched by Capitalize Albany Corporation on May 28 -- seeking ideas from real estate developers on the redevelopment of the Liberty Park site. The plans for the site are currently unclear. In the meantime, Macri said preserving these buildings is urgent.
“The more we lose historic buildings like this, the more we kind of lose that flair of Albany, and that’s a loss for everybody," said Macri.
The Historic Albany Foundation is currently working on restoring the oldest standing building in Albany, at 48 Hudson Ave. It was built in 1728 and has been vacant since 1996. Macri said she anticipates it will be ready for occupancy by this December -- where it will become the new Historic Albany Foundation headquarters.

ALBANY, N.Y. (
NEWS10
) -- An Albany man was sentenced on Thursday to over a decade in prison for the shooting that led to the death of Sky Lemmons-Dixon on Christmas Day in 2023. The Albany County District Attorney's Office said Patrick Dean, 38, shot Lemmons-Dixon in the head while inside a State Street apartment.
Get the latest news, weather, sports and entertainment delivered right to your inbox!
Dean pleaded guilty to second-degree manslaughter, second-degree criminal possession of a weapon, and tampering with evidence, in turn receiving a sentence of 16 years and four months to 19 years in state prison. Lemmons-Dixon
died at Albany Medical Center
on January 1, 2024.
The DA's office said Dean was in his apartment with Lemmons-Dixon and two friends, Ibrahim Hammond, 40, and
Michael Varlack, 37,
when Lemmons-Dixon was shot. Dean was wielding a gun when it fired and struck Lemmons-Dixon.
Trial for Albany dirt bike hit-and-run set to begin in August
Varlack pleaded guilty to third-degree criminal possession of a weapon and was sentenced to six years in prison in December 2024. Hammond pleaded guilty to first-degree perjury for his involvement in the shooting and faces a sentence of two years and four months to seven years in prison when he is sentenced on June 18.
During Dean's sentencing, Deputy Chief Assistant District Attorney Jessica Blain-Lewis read four victim impact statements from members of Lemmon-Dixon's family. Older sister Zoë Lemmons-Hall said she and Sky shared a special bond, and she was always there when life got tough.
“There aren’t enough words to accurately describe the impact of losing your baby sister,” she wrote. “Losing her has been an indescribable horror, and I’ll carry her absence with me for the rest of my life.”

content: Kamal Haasan’s Thug Life, directed by Mani Ratnam, is facing significant hurdles both at the box office and in Karnataka, where the film remains banned due to a language controversy. The makers have accused the Karnataka government of failing to address threats from pro-Kannada groups, exacerbating the film’s challenges. The controversy erupted at the Thug Life audio launch in Chennai, where Haasan remarked, “Kannada was born out of Tamil.” This statement sparked outrage among Karnataka’s pro-Kannada organizations, leading to a ban on the film’s release by the Karnataka Film Chamber of Commerce. Fringe groups have allegedly threatened violence, including burning theatres and targeting Tamil minorities. The makers have taken the issue to the Supreme Court, alleging that no FIRs have been filed despite these threats. Advocate A Velan stated, “The state government has not acted, adopting the position of the fringe elements.” The Supreme Court issued a notice to Karnataka’s Chief Secretary, Principal Secretary (Home), and Director General of Police, with a hearing set for 17 June. In response to the backlash, Haasan wrote to the Karnataka Film Chamber of Commerce, clarifying that his statement was misinterpreted and intended to promote unity. However, he refused to apologize, standing firm on his remarks. Meanwhile, Thug Life is struggling at the box office, earning Rs. 44.75 crore nett in India by its ninth day, falling short of the anticipated Rs. 50 crore mark. The film, a reunion of Haasan and Ratnam after their 1987 classic Nayakan, opened strongly on 5 June with Rs. 15.5 crore but saw a sharp 55% drop to Rs. 7.5 crore on day two. Negative reviews, competition from Akshay Kumar’s Housefull 5, and the Karnataka ban have significantly impacted its performance. Tamil occupancy dropped to 15.21% by day eight, and total collections lag behind Haasan’s Indian 2 (Rs. 70.4 crore in its first week) and Ratnam’s Ponniyin Selvan films. The Karnataka ban alone is estimated to have cost Rs. 35-40 crore in potential revenue, according to trade reports. Thug Life, a gangster drama about an aging criminal seeking vengeance, boasts a strong cast including Silambarasan TR, Trisha Krishnan, and Joju George, with music by AR Rahman. Despite its technical strengths, the film’s box office trajectory suggests a challenging road ahead, marking a rare setback for the iconic actor-director duo. Netflix has acquired the film’s digital rights for Rs. 149.7 crore, with a potential streaming release in August, though no official date has been confirmed. As the legal battle and box office struggles continue, Thug Life remains a focal point of controversy and discussion. GUILDERLAND, N.Y. (
NEWS10
) -- New York Oncology Hematology (NYOH) broke ground on Thursday
on its new facility in Guilderland
. The state-of-the-art NYOH Regional Cancer Center facility will be located near Crossgates Mall at 4 Crossgates Road.
Get the latest news, weather, sports and entertainment delivered right to your inbox!
The 105,000-square-foot facility is expected to be the largest in the area. NYOH, a cancer and blood disorder treatment provider, currently operates out of several locations around the Capital Region.
"While a regional cancer center is new for the Capital District, it is modeled after programs like Dana-Farber in Boston and Sloan Kettering in New York," said Todd Doyle, MD, President of the NYOH Board of Directors." We partner with them all the time, but this will now be creating the same patient experience here in Albany with everything under one roof."
Albany Medical Center fined $375K by NYS Department of Health
The NYOH Regional Cancer Center will have about 35 medical providers, including oncologists, hematologists and Advanced Practice Providers, to provide medical and radiation oncology services and care for malignant and benign hematology conditions. A laboratory and a pharmacy with a drive-through will also be located on-site.
When the center opens, NYOH’s three suites on Patroon Creek Boulevard in Albany will close but its other other Capital Region locations will stay open. The new Guilderland facility is projected to be completed in December 2026.

COLONIE, N.Y. (
NEWS10
) -- The Colonie Police Department held a meeting on Thursday with local retailers about the department's new Retail Theft Unit and retail theft self-reporting system. Colonie Police Chief James Gerace said officers will be stepping up foot patrols around local businesses.
Get the latest news, weather, sports and entertainment delivered right to your inbox!
Authorities said retail theft in Colonie has nearly doubled over the past several years. Many of the thefts have been credited to organized groups who steal products and resell them for cash, said officials.
The retail theft self-reporting system makes it easier for stores to communicate with each other about potential repeat offenders. The attendees were trained on how to use the new technology.

"I understand that the challenges that we face are great, I know that," said Gerace. "But if we work together with our partners, we can ensure that if we go after these organized networks which are causing the most harm to your businesses, we can ensure that retail crime does not thrive here."
Albany County District Attorney Lee Kindlon and members of the Financial Crimes Unit were also on hand to speak with stores about the DA's renewed push to target organized retail crime in the Albany area.
